title: The desktop updater adapter imports an internal module of electron-updater and reads and clears its private fields
Packaging scripts import app-builder-lib internal modules and replace a method of its NSIS target class at run time
Windows release signing runs on a shared runner where branch code under the same account can reach the hardware token; the isolation risk is accepted, not enforced

reason: Electron supplied the window, native menus and dialogs, tray, single-instance lock, deep link and a bundled browser engine and Node runtime; the owner decided there is no desktop application, so the dsh command opens the web UI in the system browser and each of the 26 Electron features has a web or command-line equivalent or a recorded drop, the embedded browser pane and sign-in pages among the drops.

Feed check, download and installer hand-off are replaced by own code for the one dsh binary: a signed manifest verified against a compiled-in key, an optional check (off until turned on) that only shows a notice in the web UI, and the dsh update command that swaps the file; there is no desktop application to update.

With no desktop application there is no bundle and no installer; what remains is signing and notarising one dsh binary per platform and archiving it, which GoReleaser does with the operating systems' signing tools, and no packaging engine is configured through hooks.

It is the engine of electron-builder, also imported for its internal ASAR reader, NSIS target and signing helpers; a Go release has one executable per platform in a plain archive, no installer and no application archive to read.
Submission to Apple and waiting are done by GoReleaser's notarize step for the dsh binary; there is no bundle or disk image to staple, because no desktop application is built.

It downloads the Electron runtime that is packaged into the application; the Go release is one executable per target in an archive, carries no engine and has no runtime prerequisite, because the user interface runs in the user's own browser.

It packs Node and a package tree into one executable with a virtual filesystem; go build produces one executable per target and the embed package carries assets, so no packer, archive or extraction cache exists.
isSea() tells packaged execution from script execution at four call sites; a Go program has one form, and the location of the running program comes from os.Executable through one function.

Upload of installers and feed files to one vendor's object storage is replaced by GitHub release assets (dsh archives, checksum file, update manifest) published by GoReleaser and the release workflow, as the owner confirmed, keeping upstream's upload rules: verify before upload, manifest last, no blind retry.
It purges one URL from the vendor's content-delivery network after a fixed installer object was replaced in place; with release assets nothing is replaced in place, so there is nothing to purge.
Only its signature check is used; HMAC-SHA-256 over the raw body with a constant-time comparison is a few lines on crypto/hmac, crypto/sha256 and encoding/hex.

The patch stops the macOS signer from following symbolic-link aliases inside Electron's framework bundles; the Go release has no bundle and no directory walk, the files to sign are an explicit list of binaries, and never following a link while signing is a stated requirement.
The patch adds the LZMA disk-image format to the builder's validator; the Go release builds no disk image and uses no packaging engine, so no third-party validator can reject a format.

The patch removes child-process rewriting, makes native-addon extraction atomic, adds typed directory listing and a size check to the virtual filesystem and lowers Brotli quality; a compiled Go binary has none of these mechanisms, and the atomic-write lesson is kept as a requirement.
This is an npm install-script policy entry for a Squirrel.Windows helper that electron-builder pulls in; Go modules run no install scripts and the package has no place in the Go design.
This is a pnpm release-age exemption needed because a native Node addon recognises one Electron runtime fingerprint; the Go design has no Electron, no pnpm policy and no addon keyed to a runtime.

There is no update library whose internals could be imported: the dsh update command owns the download and its inactivity deadline, and no downloaded release is kept between runs, so there is no hidden state to clear.
No installer is built, so there is no installer script and no packaging engine whose internal classes could be imported or altered.
Signing steps run only in the tag-triggered release workflow inside a protected environment with required approval, where pull-request code never runs, and the key stays in hardware.

title: No desktop shell: the dsh command opens the web UI in the system browser, and each Electron feature has a web or command-line equivalent or a recorded drop (replaces electron)
There is no desktop shell; the Electron feature table is the contract for the web UI and the command line (owner decision)
The embedded browser pane and the embedded sign-in pages are dropped; links and sign-in open in the system browser (owner decision)
A second dsh start for the same home and listener reuses the running host and binds nothing; a stale runtime record is replaced
The stop decision table: nothing running, work running, inspection error or timeout, repeated request, termination signal; closing every tab stops nothing
External links open without a reference to the UI, nothing external is framed, no native bridge exists and the directory picker is owner-only
A start-up failure prints one diagnostic naming a crash-report file and exits non-zero; an unclean-exit marker offers safe mode at the next start
Every Electron feature row has an answer and every dropped row names its decision
Signing, notarisation and archiving of the one dsh binary per platform: GoReleaser with the operating systems' signing tools; no bundle and no installer (replaces the electron-builder family)
One artifact per platform, one build path, one draft release published only after verification
Signing fails closed, and keys are reachable only from the protected release workflow
Distribution format: one archive per target, no installer, no bundle, nothing registered with the operating system
Release configuration lint: publish cannot run without verification, signing needs the protected environment, one version everywhere
With a fake signer: explicit sign list, no link following, no retry of a key operation, bounded timestamp retry, no credential in output
A signed and notarised macOS dsh runs on a clean machine after a browser download
A signed Windows dsh.exe runs for a standard user, and removing it leaves the harness home untouched
Signed and notarised release binaries
Update of the one dsh binary: own signed-manifest verifier, optional notify-only check and single-file swap on the standard library (replaces electron-updater)
One signed manifest and one compiled-in key anchor every update
The web UI reports an available update and never installs one
The binary is replaced only by dsh update, and nothing checks unless asked or opted in
Staged rollout is an advisory manifest field; the vendor's mandatory-update service is not built (confirmed by the owner)
The manifest verifier refuses any changed byte, foreign key, equal or lower version and missing platform entry, and leaves no downloaded file
No request with the check off or outside the web host; schedule, joined manual check, channel switch and rollout percentage under a fake clock
No download without dsh update; confirmation required; cancel and silence limit; no host route can swap; a running host keeps running and reports a pending restart
The file swap restores the old version on any injected failure, refuses a binary it does not own and never opens the harness home
The web host's optional update check is silent when off, shows a notice when on, and shows none for a tampered or foreign-signed manifest
dsh update replaces the binary on three operating systems, leaves a running host alone and refuses a tampered or unowned binary
Single-file executable: go build with cross-compilation and the embed package (replaces @yao-pkg/pkg)
Location of the running program: os.Executable behind one function (replaces node:sea)
No virtual filesystem and no run-time extraction; what must be on disk is a sidecar or an atomic cache entry
Embedded assets equal a committed manifest, a missing asset fails start-up by name, and six targets build with cgo off
Concurrent materialisation into one cache directory yields an absent or complete file and no temporary file
A helper-mode child carries no mode selector, and an interpreter name is resolved through PATH, never to the harness
The program-location function resolves symbolic links and is the only caller of os.Executable
Release hosting: release assets published by GoReleaser and the release workflow (replaces cos-nodejs-sdk-v5)
Content-delivery cache purge (not needed: no asset is replaced in place)
The vendor-specific publisher is not built; GitHub release assets are the distribution channel (confirmed by the owner)
Publication order and verification with a fake release host: verify first, manifest last, inspect before repeating an upload
GitHub webhook signature check: HMAC-SHA-256 on the standard library (replaces @octokit/webhooks)
Signature table and fuzz test: published example, changed body or secret, wrong prefix, length and digits, empty secret
A bad signature is answered before the JSON decoder is called
